problem: End-to-end RL/IL ObjectNav agents explore poorly, plan badly over long horizons, need many samples, and overfit to training scenes by memorizing object locations and appearance. The modular Active Neural SLAM (ANS) keeps only obstacle maps and uses a goal-agnostic, coverage-maximizing policy, so it cannot learn semantic priors about where a target category is likely to be.
motivation: Finding an object such as a 'dining table' in an unseen house needs three things: object detection, a long-term episodic memory of explored and unexplored space, and learned priors about how objects are arranged relative to each other, used to decide where to explore next. Explicit maps had already improved exploration and sample efficiency (ANS). Adding semantics to such a map should let a learned policy exploit these priors, while still reusing detectors pretrained on real images.
key_idea: Build an explicit multi-channel top-down semantic map by geometrically projecting first-person Mask R-CNN predictions (refined by a map-space-supervised denoiser), and train an RL policy on this map to pick goal-conditioned long-term exploration goals that a deterministic Fast Marching planner then reaches.
insight: Most of the gain comes from making exploration goal- and semantics-aware. Replacing the goal policy with ANS's coverage policy (while keeping the semantic map) drops Gibson SR from 54.4 to 45.0, about the same as ANS (44.6). Removing the semantic channels but keeping goal-driven RL gives SR 48.8, so some priors can be learned from obstacle maps alone. Error analysis with ground-truth segmentation raises SR to 73.1, which attributes roughly 19 points to perception and roughly 27% of episodes to exploration failures. Because the learned parts (map denoiser, goal policy) operate on domain-agnostic top-down maps and perception reuses a real-image-trained Mask R-CNN, the system transfers to a real Locobot (13/20 successes), while end-to-end policies failed consistently in the real world.
method: Semantic map representation: a K×M×M grid with K = C+2 channels (obstacle, explored, one channel per semantic category) and 5 cm cells. The agent starts at the map center facing east, and pose is tracked from odometry. 15 categories are mapped, although only 6 are used as goals.

Semantic Mapping module: a frozen COCO-pretrained Mask R-CNN (ResNet50-FPN) segments the RGB frame. Depth is turned into a point cloud tagged with the predicted categories and differentiably projected into voxels, then summed over height to get obstacle, explored and per-category channels. A 5-layer FCN denoiser refines the projected map, trained with BCE loss in map space. Maps are aggregated over time via spatial transforms and channel-wise pooling, as in ANS. Training uses a FIFO buffer of 500k samples, Adam at lr 1e-4, and batch size 64.

Goal-Oriented Semantic Policy: if the goal category is already on the map, all of its cells become the long-term goal. Otherwise a network (5 conv + 3 FC layers) predicts a long-term goal in map space every u=25 steps. Its inputs are the semantic map, the agent's current and past locations, and embeddings of orientation and goal category.

Goal policy training: PPO with reward equal to the decrease in geodesic distance to the nearest goal object. Settings are 86 parallel threads (one training scene each), lr 2.5e-5, γ=0.99, entropy coefficient 0.001, and 10M training frames.

Deterministic local policy: Fast Marching Method on the obstacle channel plans a path to the long-term goal. The map is updated and the path replanned every step, issuing move_forward / turn_left / turn_right / stop. This replaces ANS's learned local policy, which performed similarly.

Habitat Challenge variant: for the 21 non-COCO goal categories, Mask R-CNN is replaced by DeepLabv3 whose final layer is retrained on all 40 MP3D categories, trained with both first-person and map-space losses.

setting.backbone: Mask R-CNN ResNet50-FPN (COCO-pretrained, frozen) for segmentation + 5-layer FCN map denoiser + CNN goal policy trained with PPO; analytical FMM local planner (DeepLabv3 with fine-tuned last layer for the Habitat Challenge entry)
setting.training_data: 86 scenes (25 Gibson tiny train + 61 MP3D train) in Habitat, 10M frames of RL/supervised map training; Mask R-CNN pretrained on MS-COCO; map loss uses Gibson tiny semantic annotations from 3D Scene Graph (15 categories) and MP3D labels (6 categories)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (640×480) + odometry pose change + goal category index
setting.action_space: low-level discrete move_forward / turn_left / turn_right / stop (long-term map goals chosen every 25 steps)
setting.privileged: noise-free depth and odometry pose in simulation (as in the CVPR 2020 challenge); ground-truth semantic segmentation only in the 'SemExp w. GT SemSeg' error-analysis variant

numbers_note: The paper prints SPL/Success as fractions (e.g. 0.544); they are converted to percent here. DTS and DTG are in meters. The main Gibson/MP3D experiments use only 6 COCO goal categories on the paper's own episodes, and the paper's 'test' splits are the Gibson tiny val and MP3D val scene sets. Only the Habitat Challenge row uses the official 21-category MP3D benchmark. The real-world result is a single 20-trial number, with qualitative figures only.
results: SemExp beats all baselines on Gibson (SR 54.4 / SPL 19.9 / DTS 1.723) and MP3D (SR 36.0 / SPL 14.4). The strongest baseline, Active Neural SLAM with a heuristic detector-based local policy, gets 44.6 / 14.5 and 32.1 / 11.9. Classical mapping with frontier exploration outperforms the end-to-end RL baselines, which overfit their training scenes. SemExp won the CVPR 2020 Habitat ObjectNav Challenge with SR 25.3 / SPL 10.2 against 18.8 / 9.9 for the runner-up, and reaches 65% SR (13/20) on a real Locobot.
limitations: Perception is a major bottleneck: ground-truth segmentation raises SR from 54.4 to 73.1, and about 27% of episodes still fail because the goal is never found.

Simulation results assume perfect depth and pose. The main experiments use only 6 COCO goal categories and a small test set (5 Gibson and 10 MP3D scenes), with a modest real-world evaluation (20 trials).
The goal object is declared found whenever the detector marks it on the map, so detector false positives or false negatives directly cause failures; there is no verification step.
